tier_reason: Peer-reviewed PTHash paper (SIGIR'21, arXiv 2104.10402, Table 5) and its mirror in the roberto-trani/mphf_benchmark README show the GOV row (175 ns/key, 2.23 bits/key, 875 s) beating CMPH's CHD (416-419 ns/key) at n=10^9 on an i9-9900K, gcc 9.2.1 -O3 -march=native. The RecSplit ALENEX'20 paper corroborates this. Not A: the public harness does not include GOV, and neither paper names the harness or JVM used for GOV.

corrections.claimed_speedup: PTHash paper Table 5 (mirrored in mphf_benchmark README), n=10^9 random 64-bit keys: GOV 175 ns/key lookup, 2.23 bits/key, 875 s construction vs CHD (CMPH) 419/417/416 ns/key at 2.17/2.07/2.01 bits/key (lambda=4/5/6) -> GOV lookup about 2.4x faster than CHD (derived from page data: 419/175, 416/175). Same table at n=10^8: GOV 110 ns/key vs CHD 204/204/197 ns/key -> about 1.8x (derived from page data). Corroborated by RecSplit paper (ALENEX 2020, arXiv 1910.06416) Table 2, 10^9 keys: GOV 210 ns/key vs CHD 447/444 ns/key (lambda=5/6), about 2.1x (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: PTHash paper: gcc 9.2.1 with -O3 -march=native (mphf_benchmark CMakeLists Release also sets -O3 -march=native). Both papers state all code is C/C++ except GOV construction, which is Java-only, so GOV lookups were presumably timed with Sux4J's C lookup code (c/mph.c). The GOV lookup harness and JVM version are not stated in the PTHash paper. The RecSplit paper states gcc 8.1.1 and Java 12.
corrections.caveats: The GOV row is not produced by the mphf_benchmark harness. Its README says GOV is excluded from the reproducible commands because GOV is Java-based. GOV construction runs in Java. GOV lookup is presumably timed via Sux4J's C lookup code, c/mph.c with c/test_mph_uint64_t.c, which the papers do not name explicitly. The measured MPHF class is GOVMinimalPerfectHashFunction. GOV3Function is a static function, not an MPHF. Java code is dual-licensed LGPL-2.1-or-later OR Apache-2.0 (GitHub reports LGPL-2.1). The c/ lookup sources carry LGPL-3.0-or-later headers. GOV uses slightly more space than CHD (2.23 vs 2.01-2.17 bits/key).

notes: Numbers match the page exactly and belong to the GOV row. CHD in the harness is bonitao/cmph (the RecSplit paper cites sourceforge cmph), so the CMPH baseline is correct. Stars (176), last commit (2026-05-08), active status and non-fork status verified via gh. Consider renaming the entry to 'GOVMinimalPerfectHashFunction' rather than 'GOV3Function'.

tier_reason: The author's own blog post states the result in prose: 25% faster than a Go map for 16 keys and 50% faster for 235,000 /usr/dict/words entries. The post gives no raw numbers, Go version, or CPU. The repo has BenchmarkMPH and BenchmarkMap in mph_test.go, but no results are published, so the evidence is first-party with partial methodology.

corrections.caveats: The 25%/50% figures are prose claims in a 2017 blog post, with no raw numbers, CPU model, or Go version for this comparison. The benchmark code exists in mph_test.go (BenchmarkMPH vs BenchmarkMap; -keys flag loads a word file), but the repo publishes no results. The benchmark does not compare equal work. Table.Query returns an index for any input and does not verify key membership, while a map lookup does compare the key. The baseline was Go's 2017 map, and Go 1.24 replaced it with a Swiss-table map, so the margin may differ today. The 20.4 vs 172 ns/op table on the same page benchmarks the toy hash2 multiplier function, not go-mph.

notes: The verbatim quote and the attribution of the ns/op table in the record are both correct. The ns/op table measures hash2 with a brute-forced multiplier, not go-mph. MIT license, 65 stars, last commit 2021-12-17 (abandoned) and non-fork status verified via gh.

tier_reason: The only numbers are code comments in PerformanceTest.java: first-party figures with no JVM version, CPU, or run setup. Nothing links them to a published report or paper. The RecSplit ALENEX paper times the C++ sux implementation, not minperf.

corrections.baseline: CHD algorithm, implementation not named in the comment. The README says performance is 'very similar' to the Sux4J CHD and GOV algorithms, so the baseline is most likely Sux4J's Java CHDMinimalPerfectHashFunction. CMPH is not mentioned anywhere.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Code comment in PerformanceTest.java: 'CHD: 2.25 bits/key, 182 nanoseconds/key'. The comment gives RecSplit with FastLongHash (leafSize=11, averageBucketSize=55) as '1.97 bits/key, 163 nanoseconds/key'. That is about 1.1x faster lookup than CHD at less space (derived from page data: 182/163). The same comment lists 'GOV: 2.32 bits/key, 132 nanoseconds/key', which is faster than minperf. At equal space (leafSize=12, averageBucketSize=26: 2.32 bits/key, 138 ns/key), minperf is still slightly slower than GOV.
corrections.workload: PerformanceTest.java micro-benchmark: random long keys (default size 100,000; key count behind the commented figures not stated), RecSplit evaluation time using the test-only FastLongHash (rotate&xor). CHD/GOV figures are recorded as comments without their run setup.
corrections.caveats: The CHD/GOV figures are hand-written code comments with no JVM, CPU, key count, or harness stated. The CHD implementation is not named; the README points to Sux4J's Java CHD, not CMPH. minperf's own 163 ns/key figure uses FastLongHash, which the source calls 'not recommended to use in the real world'. The same comment shows GOV (132 ns/key) faster than minperf. The repo also has its own Java CHD reimplementation in src/test/java/org/minperf/chd/CHD.java, a possible alternative source of the CHD figure. The README calls the library 'work in progress'.

notes: Downgraded because the claim is overstated. The baseline is misattributed to CMPH. The win uses a toy hash. The win covers only CHD; GOV in the same comment beats minperf. Tier stays C. baseline_in_list is left unchanged because list membership of Sux4J's CHD could not be checked. Apache-2.0, 173 stars and last commit 2021-02-20 (abandoned) verified via gh.
